question: The Court of Auditors’ mandate includes regularly auditing EU agencies and other bodies. The total budget of all agencies audited was EUR 5.3 billion in 2024.

Three agencies working in the field of defence (the European Defence Agency, the European Union Institute for Security Studies and the European Union Satellite Centre), which are financed by contributions from Member States and audited by other independent external auditors, are not subject to auditing by the Court of Auditors.
However, the Court of Auditors’ reports for 2023 and 2024 fail to mention one particular agency: the European Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority (HERA)1.

According to the Austrian Federal Chancellery, HERA, an EU agency, is financed to the tune of EUR 6 billion from the EU’s multiannual financial framework and the EU’s recovery instrument (NextGenerationEU); an additional EUR 24 billion comes from other EU programmes. It thus has a budget of EUR 30 billion2. HERA is therefore many times better funded than all other EU agencies combined. 1.
Why has HERA not been audited by the Court of Auditors in the past, and why is it not being audited now?
Is the size of HERA’s budget appropriate, and how does the Commission justify its opinion on the budget?
Why is HERA so much better funded than other EU agencies?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.2.2026) The Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority (HERA) is a service of the Commission, not an EU decentralised agency. HERA is fully integrated into the Commission’s administrative, financial and governance framework. The European Court of Auditors (ECA) systematically audits HERA’s budget and financial transactions as part of its audits of the Commission.

The implementation of HERA’s budget is subject to the same budgetary control procedures as the other Commission services, with ensured political accountability. HERA mobilises funds under various programmes, with budgets set by the budgetary authority.

For 2022-2027, HERA draws its budget from the EU budget with a budget initially estimated at EUR 6 billion1 and subsequently adjusted downwards by the budgetary authority as part of the midterm revision of the current multi-annual financial framework2.
1 See COM(2021) 576 of 16.09.2021. 2 See Council Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/765 of 29 February 2024 amending Regulation (EU, Euratom)
2020/2093 laying down the multiannual financial framework for the years 2021 to 2027.
